```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`taxonAlign` aligns a list of raw taxon names against a taxonomic reference -- matching
misspellings, synonyms, and names only identifiable to a higher rank (`genus sp.`) -- and then
updates each match to its current accepted name. The reference can be one of the dated reference
lists taxonAlign publishes (the Australian National Species List lists, and GBIF's Australian
animals), your own table, or any mix of these.

It's inspired by [APCalign](https://traitecoevo.github.io/APCalign/)'s approach to aligning taxon
names to the Australian Plant Census, generalised so the reference doesn't have to be APC/APNI and
the taxa don't have to be plants -- every function here works for any taxonomic rank present in your
reference, not just species. A real list of raw names is rarely all species anyway -- some
identifications only ever make it to genus, family, or a "morphospecies" code -- so every example
below deliberately mixes ranks, not just species names.

Building a reference from other sources -- the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, the Catalogue of
Life, a live GBIF fetch, a [taxadb](https://docs.ropensci.org/taxadb/) snapshot, the Australian Plant
Census, or your own table with different column names -- is the job of the companion package
[taxonAlign.dataprep](https://github.com/traitecoevo/taxonalign-dataprep), which also builds the
released lists. You only need it if you're building a reference yourself.

This vignette walks through every exported function, in the order you'd typically use them, then
puts them together into the workflow you'd actually run on a real list of names.

```{r setup}
library(taxonAlign)
library(dplyr)
```

## Choosing a taxonomic reference

Every matching/aligning function needs a taxonomic reference to match against: a released list, a
global taxonomic resource, your own table, or several combined.

### A released reference list

The simplest starting point is one of the reference lists published as taxonAlign **data
releases**: dated, fixed copies of each list, so that an alignment can be repeated exactly later by
naming the release it used. The first release contains:

| Dataset | Reference | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `"NSL_animals"` | Animals (Australian Faunal Directory) | The AFD's National Species List (NSL) export |
| `"NSL_algae"` | Algae | NSL export (AAL taxa, AANI names) |
| `"NSL_bryophytes"` | Bryophytes | NSL export (CAB taxa, ABNI names) |
| `"NSL_fungi"` | Fungi | NSL export (AFL taxa, AFNI names) |
| `"NSL_lichens"` | Lichens | NSL export (ALC taxa, ALNI names) |
| `"GBIF_AU"` | Animals recorded in Australia (GBIF) | GBIF backbone taxonomy: taxa with Australian occurrence records, plus their synonyms |

`data_release_versions()` lists the releases available, most recent first, and
`data_release_datasets()` lists what's in one, with each dataset's source, retrieval date, licence and
citation:

```{r}
#| eval: false
data_release_versions()
#> [1] "2026-10-07"
data_release_datasets("2026-10-07")
```

`load_taxonomic_resources()` loads one or more datasets. Each is downloaded the first time you use it
and stored on your computer (in `tools::R_user_dir("taxonAlign", "cache")`), so after that it loads
without downloading again, and works offline. The result can go straight into any of the matching
functions:

```{r}
#| eval: false
animals <- load_taxonomic_resources(c("NSL_animals", "GBIF_AU"))
create_taxonomic_update_lookup(c("Pardalotus striatus", "Cynthia cardui"), animals)
```

When you load more than one dataset, the order you name them in is their priority: a name found in
`"NSL_animals"` is matched there, and `"GBIF_AU"` is only used for names the AFD doesn't have.

GBIF's occurrence records include fossil specimens, so taxa GBIF flags as extinct are left out by
default, as they would otherwise produce spurious matches. GBIF's flag doesn't distinguish fossils
from recent extinctions, though (the thylacine is flagged extinct too), so `include_extinct = TRUE`
keeps everything, with an `extinct` column showing which are which.

Each NSL list combines the group's two NSL exports: the *taxon* file (accepted names and their
synonyms, with links between them) and the *names* file (every name recorded for the group). The taxon
file always takes priority; names found only in the names file are added so they can still be
recognised, but they're never "updated" to anything, since the names file doesn't link them to an
accepted name. Each release also holds the NSL exports themselves, unchanged, so every list can be
traced back to exactly what was supplied.

**Naming the release.** Without `version`, the latest release is used. To make an analysis
reproducible, name the release instead -- the same release always gives the same result:

```{r}
#| eval: false
animals <- load_taxonomic_resources("NSL_animals", version = "2026-10-07")
```

**Working offline.** A named release that has already been downloaded is loaded straight from your
computer, without going online at all. Without `version`, taxonAlign checks GitHub once per session
(with a short time limit) for the latest release; if it can't (no internet, a slow connection), it
uses the most recent release already on your computer. Releases are only published when a source
actually changes, so an older release isn't necessarily out of date.

### Download global taxonomic resources

For taxa the released lists don't cover, or a reference that covers the whole world, the companion
package [taxonAlign.dataprep](https://github.com/traitecoevo/taxonalign-dataprep) downloads the major
global taxonomic resources and reshapes them into taxonAlign's format. Install it with
`pak::pak("traitecoevo/taxonalign-dataprep")`.

| Function | Reference | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `load_CoL()` | Catalogue of Life, from [ChecklistBank](https://www.checklistbank.org) | A reference to every taxon in every kingdom (~5.5 million names) |
| `load_WCVP()` | World Checklist of Vascular Plants (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew) | Every vascular plant name worldwide (~1.45 million) |
| `generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list()` | GBIF backbone taxonomy (or ITIS, NCBI and others), from [taxadb](https://docs.ropensci.org/taxadb/)'s pre-built snapshot | A large group -- a class or a phylum -- quickly |
| `generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list()` | GBIF backbone taxonomy, fetched live from GBIF | A small group -- a genus or family -- always current |
| `filter_to_country()` | Any of the above | Keeping only the taxa GBIF has occurrence records of in one or more countries |

Each returns one table in taxonAlign's format, which goes straight into the matching functions:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(taxonAlign.dataprep)

# every vascular plant name worldwide, then only those GBIF has Australian records of
wcvp_au <- load_WCVP() |> filter_to_country("AU")
create_taxonomic_update_lookup(my_plant_names, wcvp_au)

# the Catalogue of Life, pinned to one release (COL26.10) so the alignment can be repeated
col <- load_CoL(316595)

# every insect in GBIF's backbone taxonomy with an Australian occurrence record
insecta_au <- generate_taxadb_taxonomic_reference_list("Insecta", rank = "class", country = "AU")

# one genus, live from GBIF
aporocera <- generate_GBIF_taxonomic_reference_list("Aporocera", country = "AU")
```

A few things worth knowing:

- **The WCVP and Catalogue of Life are large downloads** (~90MB and ~170MB). Each is downloaded once
  and cached, so later calls load from your computer, offline. Name a version (`load_WCVP(16)`,
  `load_CoL(316595)`) to make an alignment repeatable.
- **A worldwide list matches more names than you may want**: a misspelt Australian plant name can
  fuzzy-match a species that only grows in South America. `filter_to_country()` avoids this. It keeps
  each taxon's accepted name and all its synonyms, even where GBIF and the reference disagree on which
  name is accepted, so old names in your list still update.
- **taxadb's own GBIF snapshot can be several years old.** Pass `gbif_snapshot_url` to query a current
  GBIF snapshot instead. taxadb is only needed for this one function: install it with
  `install.packages("taxadb")`.
- **For Australian vascular plants**, `load_APC()` loads the Australian Plant Census, the National
  Species List for vascular plants.

taxonAlign.dataprep's own
[getting-started vignette](https://github.com/traitecoevo/taxonalign-dataprep/blob/main/vignettes/get-started.qmd)
covers each of these in detail.

### Your own reference table

If you already have a taxonomic reference table -- your own species list, an export from a museum
database, whatever -- taxonAlign will take it as long as it's in taxonAlign's reference format: eight
required columns, `canonical_name`, `scientific_name`, `taxon_rank`, `taxonomic_status`,
`taxonomic_dataset`, `genus`, `taxon_ID` and `accepted_name_usage_ID`. `taxonomic_reference_schema()`
describes each:

```{r}
taxonomic_reference_schema() |> filter(required) |> select(column, description)
```

Here's a small, hand-built example spanning several ranks: two genera, a family, a subgenus, a species
with two synonyms (one under a different genus entirely -- a real, common pattern when a species is
reclassified over its taxonomic history), and a subspecies.

```{r}
my_reference <- tibble::tribble(
  ~scientific_name,                          ~canonical_name,             ~taxon_rank,  ~taxonomic_status, ~taxonomic_dataset, ~genus,      ~taxon_ID, ~accepted_name_usage_ID,
  "Aporocera t-viride Blackburn, 1899",       "Aporocera t-viride",       "species",    "accepted",         "MY_DATA",          "Aporocera",  "sp1",    "sp1",
  "Aporocera viridipennis Lea, 1915",         "Aporocera viridipennis",   "species",    "synonym",          "MY_DATA",          "Aporocera",  "sp2",    "sp1",
  "Chalcolampra viridis Blackburn, 1897",     "Chalcolampra viridis",     "species",    "synonym",          "MY_DATA",          "Chalcolampra", "sp3",  "sp1",
  "Aporocera Blackburn",                      "Aporocera",                "genus",      "accepted",         "MY_DATA",          NA,           "g1",     "g1",
  "Aporocera (Aporocera) Blackburn",          "Aporocera",                "subgenus",   "accepted",         "MY_DATA",          "Aporocera",  "sg1",    "sg1",
  "Chrysomelidae Latreille",                  "Chrysomelidae",           "family",     "accepted",         "MY_DATA",          NA,           "f1",     "f1",
  "Xylotoles Pascoe",                          "Xylotoles",                "genus",      "accepted",         "MY_DATA",          NA,           "g2",     "g2",
  "Xylotoles costatus Pascoe, 1859",          "Xylotoles costatus",      "species",    "accepted",         "MY_DATA",          "Xylotoles",  "sp4",    "sp4",
  "Xylotoles costatus mixtus Someone, 1920",  "Xylotoles costatus mixtus", "subspecies", "accepted",       "MY_DATA",          "Xylotoles",  "sp5",    "sp5"
)

check_taxonomic_reference(my_reference)
```

`check_taxonomic_reference()` confirms the table is in the format (it errors, listing every problem,
if it isn't) -- worth running on any reference you're going to share.

You can pass a table like this straight to the matching functions, but for repeated use it's worth
preparing it once with `prepare_taxonomic_resources()`, which the matching functions otherwise do
themselves on every call:

```{r}
resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(my_reference)
names(resources)
```

`prepare_taxonomic_resources()` splits the combined table into a nested list -- one element per
taxonomic rank present (here: `species`, `genus`, `subgenus`, `family`), with `species` further split
into `accepted`/`synonym` sub-tables. This is the shape every other function in the package works on.

Note that `my_reference` above gives an explicit `"genus"`-rank row for both `"Aporocera"` and
`"Xylotoles"` -- but you don't actually have to. Naming a genus in the `genus` column of a species row
is enough on its own: `prepare_taxonomic_resources()` automatically adds a genus-rank row for any genus
(or any other rank you record in its own column, e.g. `family`) that's implied this way but doesn't yet
have an explicit row of its own, so `"Xylotoles sp. 1"` would still align to genus rank even if the
`"Xylotoles"` row above were deleted. Synthesised rows get a placeholder ID
(`taxonomic_dataset_taxon_rank_canonical_name`, e.g. `"MY_DATA_genus_Xylotoles"`) since there's no
natural ID to reuse.

If your table's columns have other names, `taxonAlign.dataprep::build_taxonomic_reference()` walks
you through mapping them onto the format (in the style of `traits.build`'s `metadata_add_traits()`).

### Combining several references

`prepare_taxonomic_resources()` (and the matching functions) also accept a list of tables, combining
them with a priority order: when the same name appears in more than one table, whichever table is
listed *first* wins. This is how you'd combine released lists with your own data:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# your own list first, then the AFD, then GBIF for anything neither of those has
resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(c(
  list(mine = my_reference),
  load_taxonomic_resources(c("NSL_animals", "GBIF_AU"))
))
```

## Matching raw names: `align_taxa()`

`align_taxa()` takes one or more raw taxon names and matches each against `resources`, trying (in
order) exact matches, then progressively more lenient fuzzy matches, at species level first and then
at each higher rank present in `resources`.

```{r}
align_taxa("Aporocera viridipennis", resources)  # exact match, a synonym
align_taxa("Aporocera viridipenis", resources)   # one letter missing -- fuzzy match
align_taxa("Xylotoles costatus mixtus", resources) # a subspecies
align_taxa("Chrysomelidae", resources)            # family only
```

A subgenus can be written into a name or left out; either way matches, whichever way your reference
writes it:

```{r}
align_taxa(c("Aporocera t-viride", "Aporocera (Aporocera) t-viride"), resources) |>
  select(original_name, aligned_name, taxon_rank)
```

A name that can't be resolved to anything is left `NA`, not an error:

```{r}
align_taxa("Completely unrelated nonsense", resources)
```

### Matching more than one name at once

`align_taxa()` is vectorised -- pass as many names as you like in one call, spanning as many different
ranks as your raw data actually has:

```{r}
align_taxa(
  c("Aporocera t-viride", "Aporocera viridipenis", "Xylotoles costatus mixtus", "Chrysomelidae", "Xylotoles sp. 1"),
  resources
) |>
  select(original_name, aligned_name, taxon_rank)
```

In practice your names usually live in a column of a data frame, not a bare vector -- just pass that
column straight in:

```{r}
field_data <- tibble(
  name = c("Aporocera t-viride", "Chalcolampra viridis", "Xylotoles sp. 1", "Totally unknown beetle"),
  site = c("Site A", "Site B", "Site C", "Site B")
)

align_taxa(field_data$name, resources) |>
  select(original_name, aligned_name, taxon_rank, taxonomic_status)
```

Two opt-in parameters handle names that structurally can't specify a species at all, resolving them to
genus rank instead of leaving them to (possibly mis-)match a species-level pattern:

```{r}
align_taxa("Aporocera x hybridname", resources, hybrids = TRUE)
align_taxa("Aporocera aff. viridipennis", resources, intergrades_affinis = TRUE)
```

`hybrids` catches `Genus x species`-style hybrid names; `intergrades_affinis` catches intergrades
(`--`), a collector's indecision between two taxa (`/`), and graded/uncertain identifications
(`aff.`/`cf.`). Both default to `FALSE`.

A third opt-in parameter, `consider_english_name_endings`, recognises an informal vernacular ending
(e.g. `"Coccinellid"` for family Coccinellidae, `"Curculionoid"` for superfamily Curculionoidea) and
tries an exact match on the formal Latin equivalent before falling back to fuzzy matching -- useful
for the kind of morphospecies/voucher code that names a broader group this way rather than a genus:

```{r}
align_taxa("Chrysomelid sp. 1", resources, consider_english_name_endings = TRUE) |>
  select(original_name, aligned_name, taxon_rank)
```

For a large list, `progress = TRUE` prints a text progress bar tracking how many names have been
resolved so far.

Every result also includes `chars_changed` -- how many characters differed between the name and
whatever it matched: `0` for an exact match, the actual edit distance for a fuzzy one, `NA` if nothing
matched:

```{r}
align_taxa("Aporocera viridipenis", resources) |> # one letter missing
  select(original_name, aligned_name, chars_changed)
```

## Resolving to current names: `update_taxa()`

`align_taxa()` tells you *what a name matched* -- `update_taxa()` takes that result and resolves it
forward to whatever the *current* accepted name is, following synonym links via
`accepted_name_usage_ID`. This works the same way regardless of rank -- a species-level synonym and a
higher-rank one both resolve via the same lookup:

```{r}
aligned <- align_taxa(c("Chalcolampra viridis", "Xylotoles sp. 1"), resources)
update_taxa(aligned, resources) |>
  select(original_name, aligned_name, accepted_name, taxonomic_status)
```

`accepted_name` is the current accepted name (`NA` if it couldn't be resolved); `suggested_name` falls
back to `aligned_name` when there's no `accepted_name`, so it's never `NA` for anything that matched at
all.

### A synonym of more than one taxon

Sometimes a name is listed as a synonym of two or more accepted taxa -- for example, when a species
has since been split into several. The name alone can't say which is meant. Following APCalign's
convention, `update_taxa()` suggests the most likely one (by the synonyms' taxonomic status, then a
few tie-breaking rules) and lists the others in brackets, and in `alternative_possible_names`:

```{r}
split_reference <- tibble::tribble(
  ~canonical_name,        ~scientific_name,                   ~taxon_rank, ~taxonomic_status,     ~genus,       ~taxon_ID, ~accepted_name_usage_ID,
  "Newgenus alba",        "Newgenus alba (Smith, 1900)",      "species",   "accepted",            "Newgenus",   "a1",      "a1",
  "Newgenus pallida",     "Newgenus pallida Jones, 1950",     "species",   "accepted",            "Newgenus",   "a2",      "a2",
  "Oldgenus alba",        "Oldgenus alba Smith, 1900",        "species",   "nomenclatural synonym", "Oldgenus", "s1",      "a1",
  "Oldgenus alba",        "Oldgenus alba Smith, 1900",        "species",   "misapplied",          "Oldgenus",   "s2",      "a2"
) |>
  mutate(taxonomic_dataset = "EXAMPLE")

create_taxonomic_update_lookup("Oldgenus alba", prepare_taxonomic_resources(split_reference)) |>
  select(original_name, suggested_name, alternative_possible_names)
```

With `taxonomic_splits = "collapse_to_higher_taxon"`, a name whose candidates all share a genus is
reported at genus rank instead (`"Newgenus sp. [collapsed names: ...]"`).

## The one-call pipeline: `create_taxonomic_update_lookup()`

Most of the time you want both steps together. `create_taxonomic_update_lookup()` runs `align_taxa()`
then `update_taxa()` in one call:

```{r}
create_taxonomic_update_lookup(
  c("Aporocera viridipennis", "Aporocera viridipenis", "Chalcolampra viridis", "Xylotoles costatus mixtus", "Chrysomelidae"),
  resources
) |>
  select(original_name, aligned_name, accepted_name, taxonomic_status, update_reason)
```

## Putting it together: updating a list of names

Here's the workflow you'd actually run on a real list of raw names -- say, taxon names recorded in a
field dataset that need reconciling against a reference before analysis, spanning several ranks and
including a couple of names nothing will match.

```{r}
field_data <- tibble(
  original_name = c(
    "Aporocera viridipennis",   # a synonym
    "Aporocera viridipenis",    # typo
    "Xylotoles costatus mixtus", # a subspecies
    "Chrysomelidae",             # family only
    "Aporocera sp. 1",          # morphospecies code -- genus known, species not
    "Totally unknown beetle"    # won't resolve to anything
  ),
  site = c("Site A", "Site B", "Site A", "Site C", "Site B", "Site B")
)

lookup <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(field_data$original_name, resources, identifier = field_data$site)
lookup |> select(original_name, identifier, suggested_name, taxonomic_status, update_reason)
```

`identifier` (here, `site`) is threaded through so that a name only ever resolvable to genus rank (like
the morphospecies code above) is disambiguated per dataset/location in its aligned name, rather than
collapsing two genuinely different unidentified morphospecies from different sites into one.

Join the lookup back onto your original data by `original_name` to get an updated name for every row:

```{r}
field_data |> left_join(lookup, by = "original_name")
```

From here, the rows worth a closer look are the ones where `taxonomic_status` is `"unknown"` (nothing
matched at all) or `suggested_name` is `NA` -- everything else resolved to *something*, even if only at
a higher rank. Reviewing exactly those rows (rather than the whole list) is usually the fastest way to
find the handful of names that need a manual look -- a real typo not caught by fuzzy matching, a name
missing from your reference entirely, or a genuinely new/undescribed taxon.

```{r}
lookup |> filter(is.na(suggested_name) | taxonomic_status == "unknown")
```
